title: Plasmalemma vesicle-associated protein in hepatic stellate cells is a central regulator of hepatic fatty acid utilization
projectDescription: The liver is essential for fatty acid utilization during fasting. Fatty acids released by lipolysis from adipose tissue during fasting are taken up from the blood by hepatocytes and esterified as triacylglycerols for oxidative metabolization and ketogenesis. Whereas the regulation of fatty acid oxidation in hepatocytes is well understood, transport of non-esterified fatty acids (NEFAs) from the liver sinusoidal lumen to the hepatocyte is not. Here, we show that murine hepatic stellate cells (HSCs), enveloping the liver sinusoids as pericytes, and their abundantly expressed plasmalemma vesicle-associated protein (PLVAP) control hepatic NEFA uptake during fasting. HSC-specific ablation of PLVAP suppresses hepatocyte fatty acid esterification to di- and triacylglycerols along with fasting fatty acid utilization and ketogenesis. Consistently, single cell-resolved transcriptomics further revealed severe perturbation of hepatocyte gene programs governing normal fatty acid handling, oxidation, and ketogenesis. By super-resolution microscopy we localized HSC PLVAP to caveolae residing along the sinusoidal lumen strongly supporting a role for PLVAP in caveolar transcytosis of NEFAs across HSCs and hence the sinusoid wall as rate-limiting for hepatic fatty acid utilization during fasting. This was supported by a similar decline in neutral lipid droplet formation in livers of fasting Caveolin-1 knockout mice. Altogether, our study shows vital roles for PLVAP and for HSCs in normal fasting metabolism of liver.
sampleProcessingProtocol: 100 μg isolated serum were reduced with 2 mM dithiothreitol at RT for 45 min., alkylated with 11 mM iodoacetamide in the dark at room temperature for 60 min., then digested with Lys-C for 2 hours and added 1 μg of modified trypsin (Promega, Madison, USA) for 18 hours at 37°C. After digestion, the sample was acidified to 0.1% trifluoracetic acid (TFA), final concentration, and desalted with homemade microcolumns StageTip made using a P200 pipette tip plugged with two C18 discs. Peptide concentration was measured using a nanodrop. ~1 μg of the tryptic digested sample was applied into an analytical column (New Objective x 75 μm internal diameter x 1.9 μm particle size ReproSil-Pur 120 C18-AQ, DR. MAISCH) which was heated to 50°C using a column heater. Separation of the samples by liquid chromatography (LC) prior to injection into the mass spectrometer was conducted using an Easy-nLC 1200 system (Thermo Scientific) coupled to an Exploris 480 mass spectrometry (Thermo Scientific). Data were obtained using Xcalibur software (version 4.4.16.14).
dataProcessingProtocol: For data analysis, the correlation between conditions were calculated after removal of all missing values across conditions and Pearson correlation coefficient (rp) was applied in order to check statistical differences. Generated mass spectrometry data was searched using DIA-NN 1.8.1 against a FASTA file downloaded from UniProt in September 2022. The parameters used for the search included carbamidomethylation of cysteines as a fixed modification and the variable modifications methionine oxidation and N-terminal acetylation. Trypsin was used as the digestive enzyme, missed cleavages were set to a maximum of two and a default false discovery rate (FDR) of 0.01 was used. The main search peptide tolerance was set to 10 ppm. The quantified peptide abundances were exported from DIA-NN for statistical analysis. Then, the data were imported into R and analyzed with the pmartR package  for quality control and statistical analysis. The data were log2 transformed and the peptides filtered. Peptide filters were based on the presence of degenerate peptides, presence of missing values and susceptibility to ANOVA and g-test. Peptides identified for more than one protein, peptides with less than 75% quantitation across all the samples and peptides not susceptible to ANOVA or g-test were excluded. Protein rollup was performed with the Rollup tool in pmartR with default parameters. Comparisons subjected to the independence of missing data and statistical tests ANOVA (IMD-ANOVA) were submitted to robust Mahalanobis distance analysis for outlier diagnosis (RMD), based on median absolute deviation (MAD), asymmetry, correlation, and proportion of missing values. Then, the abundance data were normalized according to the SPANS tool present in pmartR.
